rich_summary: In this interpolated chapter of the Uttara Kanda, the sage Sanatkumara speaks with Ravana and reveals the supreme nature of Narayana. He describes the deity as the all‑pervading, eternal reality present throughout the three worlds—creator, sustainer, and destroyer of all existence. Narayana’s divine form is portrayed in radiant imagery, adorned with the Srivatsa mark and accompanied by Lakshmi. The sage explains that the Supreme cannot be seen through ritual or sacrifice alone but only through complete surrender and purified understanding. He then delivers a prophetic revelation: at the end of the Golden Age, Narayana will incarnate as Rama, son of Dasaratha, while Lakshmi will appear as Sita, born from the earth. Hearing this, Ravana begins plotting how he might confront this future incarnation, foreshadowing the central conflict of the epic.

highlight_spans.why: Sanatkumara’s declaration of the supreme, all‑pervading nature of the deity establishes the theological core of the passage.
The prophecy that Narayana will incarnate in human form marks the pivotal mythic revelation leading to Rama’s birth.
The explicit identification of Rama as the future son of Dasaratha anchors the prophecy in the epic’s main narrative.
The introduction of Sita as Lakshmi incarnate and born from the earth emphasizes the sacred union central to the story.

top_scenes.scene_text: The radiant sage Sanatkumara revealing the cosmic form of Narayana to Ravana, the three worlds symbolically surrounding them as the god’s presence fills sky, earth, and underworld.
A prophetic vision of Narayana descending into human form as the future prince Rama, blazing like the sun while gods watch from the heavens.
Sita emerging from the earth in a field of light while Rama stands beside her, the pair glowing like the sun and its rays.
